setting: Examples use a small online shop: orders, products, customers, web sessions, refunds, and a table of metric definitions.

words.name: Measure
words.meaning: One sum, count or other total over Facts.
words.example: total revenue = sum of order amount

words.name: Metric
words.example: revenue growth = (this year's revenue - last year's revenue) / last year's revenue

tables:
SQL and DAX:  order_items / Items (order_id, customer_id, product_id, unit_price, quantity, sale_price, status, order_date, ship_date)
              sale_price is the value of the line: unit_price x quantity
              products (product_id, brand, category, cost)   cost is for one unit
              customers (customer_id, city, region, tier)   customer_history (customer_id, tier, valid_from, valid_to)
              sessions (session_id, session_date)   stock (product_id, snapshot_date, units_on_hand)   budget (month, amount)
              refunds / Refunds (refund_id, order_id, amount, refund_date)
              metric_definitions / Defs (metric_id, name, idea, formula, version, status, valid_from, valid_to)
              status is active, retired or superseded (an older version of a definition that changed)
              calendar (date), one row for each date   calendar_months (month), one row for each month
Excel:        one flat table called Items, with the product and customer columns, and month and year, already looked up
              plus Daily (date, sales) with a row for every date, Stock, Sessions, History, Refunds and Defs

families.name: Simple totals
families.description: One total over one list of rows. Every layer starts here.

families.name: Totals with a rule inside
families.description: The business rule lives in the definition, so nobody has to remember it.

families.name: Formulas over totals
families.description: Two or more Measures combined. The parts must be totalled first, then combined.

families.name: Compared with a whole
families.description: The number only means something beside a bigger number.

families.name: Over time
families.description: The same Measure, seen through a period. Time causes more wrong numbers than anything else.

families.name: Things that do not add up
families.description: Numbers that are right at each level, and wrong when the levels are added.

families.name: Across more than one list of events
families.description: The question needs two kinds of event, or events about events.

families.name: Definitions that people can trust
families.description: The arithmetic can be right and the number still wrong, because nobody can say which definition gave it.

patterns.name: Sum
patterns.whatItIs: Add up a recorded value.
patterns.plainExample: total sales = sum of sale price
patterns.question: What are our total sales?
patterns.layerMust: Add every row once, including rows that have no match in another table.
patterns.withoutIt: A total that quietly loses rows.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
examples.dax: Total Sales = SUM ( Items[sale_price] )

patterns.name: Count
patterns.whatItIs: Count the rows, or count a key.
patterns.plainExample: items sold = count of order items
patterns.question: How many items did we sell?
patterns.layerMust: Know what one row is.
patterns.withoutIt: A count of the wrong thing, such as orders when items were asked.

examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM order_items
examples.dax: Items Sold = COUNTROWS ( Items )

patterns.name: Distinct count
patterns.whatItIs: Count each different thing once.
patterns.plainExample: buyers = count of different customers
patterns.question: How many customers bought from us?
patterns.layerMust: Count people, not rows.
patterns.withoutIt: A customer with two orders counts twice.

examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
FROM order_items
examples.dax: Buyers = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[customer_id] )

patterns.name: Smallest and largest
patterns.whatItIs: The lowest or highest value, or the earliest or latest date.
patterns.plainExample: first order date = earliest order date
patterns.question: When did we get our first order? What was our biggest sale?
patterns.layerMust: Work on dates as well as numbers.
patterns.withoutIt: People export the data to find it.

examples.sql:
SELECT MIN(order_date), MAX(sale_price)
FROM order_items
examples.dax:
First Order Date = MIN ( Items[order_date] )
Biggest Sale = MAX ( Items[sale_price] )

patterns.name: Average of a value
patterns.whatItIs: The mean of a recorded value.
patterns.plainExample: average sale price = average of sale price
patterns.question: What does a typical item sell for?
patterns.layerMust: Average the rows, not other averages.
patterns.withoutIt: An average of averages, which is a different number.

examples.sql:
SELECT AVG(sale_price)
FROM order_items
examples.dax: Average Sale Price = AVERAGE ( Items[sale_price] )

patterns.name: Middle value
patterns.whatItIs: The median, or another percentile.
patterns.plainExample: median order value
patterns.question: What does a normal order look like, without the few huge ones?
patterns.layerMust: Offer more than sum, count and average.
patterns.withoutIt: A mean that a few large orders pull upward.

examples.sql:
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)
       WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY order_value)
FROM (SELECT order_id, SUM(sale_price) AS order_value
      FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) o
examples.dax:
Median Order Value =
MEDIANX ( VALUES ( Items[order_id] ),
          CALCULATE ( SUM ( Items[sale_price] ) ) )

patterns.name: Filtered measure
patterns.whatItIs: A total with a condition built in.
patterns.plainExample: completed sales = sum of sale price where status is complete
patterns.question: What are our completed sales?
patterns.layerMust: Hold the filter in the definition.
patterns.withoutIt: Each person applies the filter their own way, or forgets it.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
WHERE status = 'Complete'
examples.dax:
Completed Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], Items[status] = "Complete" )

patterns.name: Default exclusions
patterns.whatItIs: A total that leaves out a standard list.
patterns.plainExample: net sales = sales without cancelled and returned items
patterns.question: What are our net sales?
patterns.layerMust: Hold a list of things to leave out.
patterns.withoutIt: Test orders and cancellations in the board report.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled','Returned')
examples.dax:
Net Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  NOT Items[status] IN { "Cancelled", "Returned" } )

patterns.name: Conditional count
patterns.whatItIs: Count only the rows that meet a condition.
patterns.plainExample: returned items = count where status is returned
patterns.question: How many items came back?
patterns.layerMust: Put a condition inside the count.
patterns.withoutIt: A second table built only to count one status.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Returned'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
FROM order_items
examples.dax:
Returned Items =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( Items ), Items[status] = "Returned" )

patterns.name: Ratio
patterns.whatItIs: One Measure divided by another.
patterns.plainExample: average order value = total sales / order count
patterns.question: What is our average order value?
patterns.layerMust: Divide the totals, at every level of a report.
patterns.withoutIt: The overall figure is the average of the rows above it.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
FROM order_items
examples.dax:
Average Order Value =
DIVIDE ( [Total Sales], DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[order_id] ) )

patterns.name: Rate
patterns.whatItIs: A part divided by its whole, as a percentage.
patterns.plainExample: return rate = returned items / items sold
patterns.question: What is our return rate?
patterns.layerMust: Keep the top and bottom numbers from the same set of rows.
patterns.withoutIt: A rate above 100%.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Returned'
                THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)
FROM order_items
examples.dax: Return Rate = DIVIDE ( [Returned Items], [Items Sold] )

patterns.name: Ratio across two tables
patterns.whatItIs: The parts sit in different tables.
patterns.plainExample: margin = (sales - product cost) / sales
patterns.question: What is our gross margin?
patterns.layerMust: Fetch each item's cost from the product table, and lose or repeat no item on the way.
patterns.withoutIt: Items with no matching product drop out, and margin looks better than it is.

examples.sql:
-- LEFT JOIN keeps every item. An item with no product
-- has no cost: find those items, never count them as 0.
SELECT (SUM(i.sale_price) - SUM(p.cost * i.quantity))
       / SUM(i.sale_price)
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
examples.dax:
Gross Margin =
VAR Cost = SUMX ( Items, RELATED ( Products[cost] ) * Items[quantity] )
RETURN DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - Cost, [Total Sales] )

patterns.name: Weighted average
patterns.whatItIs: An average where bigger rows count for more.
patterns.plainExample: sum of (unit price x quantity) / sum of quantity
patterns.question: What is our average price, allowing for how many we sold?
patterns.layerMust: Multiply before adding.
patterns.withoutIt: A plain average that treats one sale like a thousand.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(unit_price * quantity) / SUM(quantity)
FROM order_items
examples.dax:
Weighted Price =
DIVIDE ( SUMX ( Items, Items[unit_price] * Items[quantity] ),
         SUM ( Items[quantity] ) )

patterns.name: Metric built from metrics
patterns.whatItIs: A metric whose parts are metrics. Often drawn as a tree.
patterns.plainExample: sales = buyers x orders per buyer x value per order
patterns.question: Sales are down. Is it fewer buyers, fewer orders each, or smaller orders?
patterns.layerMust: Let one definition use another, and keep the link.
patterns.withoutIt: The parts are defined three times and stop agreeing.

examples.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) * 1.0
    / COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS orders_per_buyer,
  SUM(sale_price)
    / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS value_per_order
FROM order_items
examples.excel:
=Buyers*OrdersPerBuyer*ValuePerOrder
(three named cells, each with its own formula)
examples.dax:
Orders = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[order_id] )
Orders per Buyer = DIVIDE ( [Orders], [Buyers] )
Sales From Parts =
[Buyers] * [Orders per Buyer] * [Average Order Value]

patterns.name: Share of total
patterns.whatItIs: A part over the whole, where the whole ignores the split.
patterns.plainExample: brand share = brand sales / all sales
patterns.question: What share of sales does each brand have?
patterns.layerMust: Work out the bottom number at a wider level than the rows.
patterns.withoutIt: Every brand shows 100%.

examples.sql:
SELECT p.brand,
  SUM(i.sale_price)
    / SUM(SUM(i.sale_price)) OVER () AS share
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
GROUP BY p.brand
examples.dax:
Brand Share =
DIVIDE ( [Total Sales],
  CALCULATE ( [Total Sales], ALL ( Products[brand] ) ) )

patterns.name: A wider total on narrower rows
patterns.whatItIs: Two levels of total in one answer.
patterns.plainExample: city sales, region sales, side by side
patterns.question: Show each city's sales beside its region's total.
patterns.layerMust: Total at two levels in one query.
patterns.withoutIt: Two reports and a spreadsheet to join them.

examples.sql:
SELECT c.region, c.city,
  SUM(i.sale_price) AS city_sales,
  SUM(SUM(i.sale_price))
    OVER (PARTITION BY c.region) AS region_sales
FROM order_items i
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = i.customer_id
GROUP BY c.region, c.city
examples.dax:
Region Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  ALLEXCEPT ( Customers, Customers[region] ) )

patterns.name: Top N and rank
patterns.whatItIs: Order by a Measure and keep the first few.
patterns.plainExample: top 3 brands by sales
patterns.question: Who are our top 3 brands?
patterns.layerMust: Rank on a total, and say what happens in a tie.
patterns.withoutIt: Two brands tie for third and one vanishes.

examples.sql:
WITH b AS (
  SELECT p.brand, SUM(i.sale_price) AS sales,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(i.sale_price) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM order_items i
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
  GROUP BY p.brand)
SELECT brand, sales, rnk
FROM b
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk
examples.dax:
Brand Rank =
RANKX ( ALL ( Products[brand] ), [Total Sales] )
(then keep the brands where the rank is 3 or less)

patterns.name: Time window
patterns.whatItIs: A total over a moving period.
patterns.plainExample: sales, last 30 days
patterns.question: What were sales in the last 30 days?
patterns.layerMust: Know which date to use, and what today is.
patterns.withoutIt: A window that filters nothing, so all sales come back.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
WHERE order_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
examples.dax:
Sales Last 30 Days =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  DATESINPERIOD ( Calendar[date],
    MAX ( Calendar[date] ), -30, DAY ) )

patterns.name: Period to date
patterns.whatItIs: A total from the start of a period to now.
patterns.plainExample: sales, year to date
patterns.question: How are we doing this year so far?
patterns.layerMust: Know where a period starts, including a financial year.
patterns.withoutIt: The calendar year used where the financial year was meant.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
WHERE order_date >= DATE_TRUNC('year', CURRENT_DATE)
  AND order_date <= CURRENT_DATE
examples.dax:
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD ( [Total Sales], Calendar[date] )
Sales FYTD =
TOTALYTD ( [Total Sales], Calendar[date], "31/3" )
(a financial year that ends on 31 March)

patterns.name: Period over period
patterns.whatItIs: This period against the same period before.
patterns.plainExample: growth = (this year - last year) / last year
patterns.question: How much did sales grow on last year?
patterns.layerMust: Line up like with like, including a part-finished month and a leap day.
patterns.withoutIt: Half a month compared with a full month.

examples.sql:
WITH y AS (
  SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) AS yr,
         SUM(sale_price) AS sales
  FROM order_items GROUP BY 1)
SELECT yr,
  sales / LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY yr) - 1 AS growth
FROM y
examples.dax:
Sales Growth =
VAR LastYear = CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( Calendar[date] ) )
RETURN DIVIDE ( [Total Sales] - LastYear, LastYear )

patterns.name: Running total
patterns.whatItIs: Each period added to all the ones before.
patterns.plainExample: cumulative sales by month
patterns.question: How have sales built up through the year?
patterns.layerMust: Add across rows in order.
patterns.withoutIt: The running total restarts or skips.

examples.sql:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
  SUM(SUM(sale_price)) OVER (
    ORDER BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)) AS running
FROM order_items
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
examples.dax:
Running Sales =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  FILTER ( ALL ( Calendar[date] ),
    Calendar[date] <= MAX ( Calendar[date] ) ) )

patterns.name: Rolling average
patterns.whatItIs: The average of the last few periods, moving along.
patterns.plainExample: 7-day average sales
patterns.question: What is the trend, without the daily noise?
patterns.layerMust: Look back a fixed number of periods from each row.
patterns.withoutIt: The first rows average over too few days and nobody is told.

examples.sql:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT c.date, COALESCE(SUM(i.sale_price), 0) AS sales
  FROM calendar c
  LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_date = c.date
  GROUP BY c.date)
SELECT date,
  CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER w = 7
       THEN AVG(sales) OVER w END AS avg_7
FROM daily
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY date
  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
examples.excel:
=AVERAGEIFS(Daily[sales],
  Daily[date],">"&[@date]-7,
  Daily[date],"<="&[@date])
(Daily has a row for every date, with 0 on a day with no sales)
examples.dax:
Sales 7 Day Average =
DIVIDE (
  CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
    DATESINPERIOD ( Calendar[date],
      MAX ( Calendar[date] ), -7, DAY ) ),
  7 )
(divide by 7 days: AVERAGEX would skip the days with no sales)

patterns.name: One measure, a second date
patterns.whatItIs: The same total placed on a different date.
patterns.plainExample: sales by ship date
patterns.question: What were sales by ship date, not order date?
patterns.layerMust: Let one Measure use more than one date.
patterns.withoutIt: A second copy of the metric for each date.

examples.sql:
SELECT ship_date, SUM(sale_price)
FROM order_items
GROUP BY ship_date
examples.dax:
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE ( [Total Sales],
  USERELATIONSHIP ( Items[ship_date], Calendar[date] ) )

patterns.name: Periods with nothing in them
patterns.whatItIs: A period with no rows must still show.
patterns.plainExample: a month with no orders shows as empty
patterns.question: Show sales for every month this year.
patterns.layerMust: Have a calendar of its own.
patterns.withoutIt: The quiet month is missing from the chart.

examples.sql:
SELECT c.month, SUM(i.sale_price) AS sales
FROM calendar_months c
LEFT JOIN order_items i
  ON DATE_TRUNC('month', i.order_date) = c.month
GROUP BY c.month
examples.excel:
=SUMIFS(Items[sale_price],Items[month],[@month])
(in a list that has a row for every month)
examples.dax:
Sales Every Month = [Total Sales] + 0
(with Calendar[month] on the rows)

patterns.name: Distinct count across a split
patterns.whatItIs: A distinct count shown with a breakdown.
patterns.plainExample: buyers by category, and all buyers
patterns.question: How many buyers in each category, and in total?
patterns.layerMust: Work out the total again, not add the rows.
patterns.withoutIt: A buyer in two categories counts twice in the total.

examples.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'No category') AS category,
  COUNT(DISTINCT i.customer_id) AS buyers
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (1)
-- the total row is the one row with no category
examples.dax:
Buyers = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[customer_id] )
(a measure is worked out again on the total row)

patterns.name: Balance at a point in time
patterns.whatItIs: A value that adds across things, and not across time.
patterns.plainExample: stock on hand at month end
patterns.question: How much stock do we hold?
patterns.layerMust: Add across products and take the last value across days.
patterns.withoutIt: Thirty days of stock added into one huge month.

examples.sql:
SELECT SUM(units_on_hand)
FROM stock
WHERE snapshot_date =
  (SELECT MAX(snapshot_date) FROM stock)
examples.dax:
Stock on Hand =
CALCULATE ( SUM ( Stock[units_on_hand] ),
  LASTNONBLANK ( Calendar[date],
    CALCULATE ( SUM ( Stock[units_on_hand] ) ) ) )

patterns.name: A total line worked out again
patterns.whatItIs: The total row of a ratio or rate.
patterns.plainExample: overall rate = all returns / all items
patterns.question: What is the return rate overall, under the rate for each category?
patterns.layerMust: Recompute the total line from totals.
patterns.withoutIt: The total line adds or averages the percentages.

examples.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'No category') AS category,
  SUM(CASE WHEN i.status = 'Returned'
           THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS rate
FROM order_items i
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (1)
-- the total row is the one row with no category
examples.excel:
Total row:
=COUNTIFS(Items[status],"Returned")/ROWS(Items)
(from all rows, not from the rates above it)
examples.dax:
Return Rate = DIVIDE ( [Returned Items], [Items Sold] )
(a measure is worked out again on the total row)

patterns.name: Two events at two levels
patterns.whatItIs: Two separate lists, each totalled on its own, then combined.
patterns.plainExample: conversion = orders / sessions
patterns.question: How many website sessions become orders?
patterns.layerMust: Total each list alone before it combines them.
patterns.withoutIt: Joining the lists multiplies both numbers.

examples.sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM order_items)
  * 1.0 /
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions) AS conversion
examples.dax:
Conversion =
DIVIDE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[order_id] ),
         COUNTROWS ( Sessions ) )

patterns.name: Actual against a target
patterns.whatItIs: Events at a fine level against a plan at a coarse level.
patterns.plainExample: sales by day against budget by month
patterns.question: Are we ahead of budget?
patterns.layerMust: Bring both to a level they share.
patterns.withoutIt: The monthly budget repeated on every day and added up.

examples.sql:
WITH a AS (
  SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(sale_price) AS sales
  FROM order_items GROUP BY 1)
SELECT COALESCE(a.month, b.month) AS month,
  COALESCE(a.sales, 0) - COALESCE(b.amount, 0)
    AS against_budget
FROM a
FULL OUTER JOIN budget b ON b.month = a.month
ORDER BY 1
examples.dax:
Sales vs Budget =
[Total Sales] - SUM ( Budget[amount] )
(both tables link to Calendar at the month)

patterns.name: A measure over a measure
patterns.whatItIs: Total once for each customer, then total those results.
patterns.plainExample: repeat rate = buyers with 2 or more orders / all buyers
patterns.question: What share of buyers buy again?
patterns.layerMust: Total in two steps.
patterns.withoutIt: The rate is counted by order, not by buyer.

examples.sql:
WITH c AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
  FROM order_items GROUP BY 1)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN orders >= 2
                THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)
FROM c
examples.dax:
Repeat Rate =
DIVIDE (
  COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( Items[customer_id] ),
    CALCULATE ( DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[order_id] ) ) >= 2 ) ),
  [Buyers] )

patterns.name: Cohort
patterns.whatItIs: Group people by when they started, then follow each group.
patterns.plainExample: month 1 retention by first-order month
patterns.question: Of the people who first bought in March, how many came back in April?
patterns.layerMust: Know each customer's first event, and tell "none" from "not yet known".
patterns.withoutIt: A month that has not happened yet shows 0%.

examples.sql:
WITH f AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
    MIN(DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)) AS first_month
  FROM order_items GROUP BY 1)
SELECT f.first_month,
  CASE WHEN f.first_month + INTERVAL '2' MONTH
            > CURRENT_DATE
       THEN NULL  -- month 1 has not finished yet
       ELSE COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
         WHEN DATE_TRUNC('month', i.order_date)
              = f.first_month + INTERVAL '1' MONTH
         THEN i.customer_id END) * 1.0
         / COUNT(DISTINCT f.customer_id)
  END AS month_1
FROM f
JOIN order_items i ON i.customer_id = f.customer_id
GROUP BY f.first_month
ORDER BY 1
examples.excel:
Helper column first_month:
=MINIFS(Items[month],Items[customer_id],[@customer_id])
Then, for each starting month:
=COUNTA(UNIQUE(FILTER(Items[customer_id],
   (Items[first_month]=[@month])
  *(Items[month]=EDATE([@month],1)))))
 /COUNTA(UNIQUE(FILTER(Items[customer_id],
   Items[first_month]=[@month])))
examples.dax:
Month 1 Retention =
VAR m = SELECTEDVALUE ( Customers[first_month] )
VAR Back = CALCULATE (
  DISTINCTCOUNT ( Items[customer_id] ),
  Items[month] = EDATE ( m, 1 ) )
RETURN DIVIDE ( Back,
  DISTINCTCOUNT ( Customers[customer_id] ) )
(uses a first_month column on Customers)

patterns.name: A detail as it was then
patterns.whatItIs: Use a value as it was on the day of the event.
patterns.plainExample: sales by tier at time of order
patterns.question: What were sales by the customer's tier at the time they bought?
patterns.layerMust: Keep history, and join to it by date.
patterns.withoutIt: Last year's sales are moved to this year's tier.

examples.sql:
SELECT h.tier, SUM(i.sale_price)
FROM order_items i
JOIN customer_history h
  ON h.customer_id = i.customer_id
 AND i.order_date >= h.valid_from
 AND i.order_date <  h.valid_to
GROUP BY h.tier
examples.dax:
Column on Items:
tier_then =
MAXX ( FILTER ( History,
    History[customer_id] = Items[customer_id]
 && History[valid_from] <= Items[order_date]
 && History[valid_to] > Items[order_date] ),
  History[tier] )
Then use [Total Sales] by Items[tier_then]

patterns.name: Two metrics that are nearly the same
patterns.whatItIs: Two saved definitions for one business idea, with a small difference between them.
patterns.plainExample: "revenue" counts every order. "net revenue" leaves out returns. Both answer "what is our revenue?"
patterns.question: Which revenue number is the right one?
patterns.layerMust: Hold one definition for one idea, or say how the two differ, so a question finds the right one.
patterns.withoutIt: Which number answers depends on luck: the first name found, or the one a person used last.

examples.sql:
-- Find ideas with more than one definition
SELECT a.idea, a.name, a.formula,
       b.name AS also, b.formula AS also_formula
FROM metric_definitions a
JOIN metric_definitions b
  ON b.idea = a.idea
 AND b.metric_id > a.metric_id
WHERE a.status = 'active'
  AND b.status = 'active'
examples.excel:
=FILTER(Defs[[name]:[formula]],
  (Defs[idea]="revenue")*(Defs[status]="active"))
(two or more rows means one idea has two definitions)
examples.dax:
EVALUATE
FILTER ( Defs,
  Defs[idea] = "revenue" && Defs[status] = "active" )
(two or more rows means one idea has two definitions.
A model's own measures carry no idea, so this needs the Defs table)

patterns.name: A retired metric
patterns.whatItIs: A definition that was right once, and is no longer the one to use.
patterns.plainExample: "active customers (old)" was replaced by "active customers" in July. Only the new one answers.
patterns.question: Is this still the number we use?
patterns.layerMust: Mark a definition as retired and stop serving it, so only the current one answers.
patterns.withoutIt: An old definition still answers, and its number looks just as trusted as the new one.

examples.sql:
-- Serve only the current definitions
CREATE VIEW served_metrics AS
SELECT metric_id, name, formula
FROM metric_definitions
WHERE status = 'active'
examples.excel:
=FILTER(Defs[name],Defs[status]="active")
(use this list, not the whole table, wherever people pick a metric)
examples.dax:
EVALUATE
FILTER ( Defs, Defs[status] = "active" )
(Power BI has no retired state for a measure.
Hiding one still lets an old report show its number)

patterns.name: A right answer of nothing
patterns.whatItIs: A question whose true answer is none, or zero.
patterns.plainExample: orders refunded twice = none
patterns.question: Which orders were refunded twice?
patterns.layerMust: Return "none" as the answer, not an error, not an empty screen and not a guess.
patterns.withoutIt: An empty result reads as a broken report, or a tool fills the gap with a number that is not there.

examples.sql:
-- Zero is the answer, so say it
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_refunded_twice
FROM (
  SELECT order_id
  FROM refunds
  GROUP BY order_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2) r
examples.dax:
Orders Refunded Twice =
COUNTROWS (
  FILTER ( VALUES ( Refunds[order_id] ),
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( Refunds ) ) >= 2 ) ) + 0
(+ 0 shows 0, not an empty cell)

patterns.name: A definition that changed
patterns.whatItIs: The same metric name, with a new formula from a date on.
patterns.plainExample: gross margin did not take off shipping before November, and does from November
patterns.question: Why is last month's margin different from what I saw last month?
patterns.layerMust: Keep each definition's history, and say which version gave a number.
patterns.withoutIt: A remembered number and today's number disagree, and nobody can say why.

examples.sql:
-- Which version applied on a date
SELECT name, version, formula
FROM metric_definitions
WHERE metric_id = 'gross_margin'
  AND DATE '2026-10-31' >= valid_from
  AND DATE '2026-10-31' <  valid_to
examples.dax:
EVALUATE
FILTER ( Defs,
  Defs[metric_id] = "gross_margin"
    && Defs[valid_from] <= DATE ( 2026, 10, 31 )
    && Defs[valid_to] > DATE ( 2026, 10, 31 ) )
(a measure cannot say which formula it had on a date,
so the history lives in the Defs table)
